chunks.arabic_text: رِجَالُ الْكَشِّيِّ: حَمْدَوَيْهُ بْنُ نَصِيرٍ، عَنِ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ عِيسَى، عَنِ الْوَشَّاءِ، عَنِ هِشَامِ بْنِ سَالِمٍ، عَنِ الزُّرَارِيِّ قَالَ

translations.en: Rijal al-Kashshi: Hamduwayh ibn Nusayr, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Washsha, from Hisham ibn Salim, from al-Zurari who said:

chunks.arabic_text: سَأَلْتُ أَبَا جَعْفَرٍ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ عَنْ جَوَائِزِ الْعُمَالِ؟ فَقَالَ: لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ، قَالَ: ثُمَّ قَالَ: إِنَّمَا أَرَادَ الزُّرَارِيُّ أَنْ يَبْلُغَ هِشَامَ أَنِّي أُحَرِّمُ أَعْمَالَ السُّلْطَانِ

translations.en: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the stipends of the officials? He said: There is no harm in it, he said: Then he said: Indeed, al-Zurari wanted that it reach Hisham that I prohibit the works of the Sultan.

en.summary: This narration from Al-Kashi’s *Rijal* highlights the subtle political dynamics between the Imams and the Umayyad Caliphate, where Imam al-Baqir (AS) permits accepting stipends (*jawā'iz*) but reveals Zurara’s deeper intent to signal disapproval of Sultanate service. This reflects the Shia scholarly principle of *al-ḥikmah* (wisdom) and *al-taqiyyah* (precaution), allowing practical engagement with authority while maintaining theological independence. The incident underscores how early Shia scholars navigated public compliance with state structures without compromising their distinct identity.
en.seo_question: What is the ruling on accepting salary from government officials in Shia jurisprudence according to Rijal al-Kashshi?

key_terms.جَوَائِزِ الْعُمَالِ: Stipends or salaries given to officials
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm in it (permissible)
